\[
\text{Let the square be }ABCD\text{ with }A(0,0),\ B(1,0),\ C(1,1),\ D(0,1).
\]

The mid–points of the sides are  

\[
M_{AB}\Bigl(\frac12,0\Bigr),\qquad 
M_{BC}\Bigl(1,\frac12\Bigr),\qquad 
M_{CD}\Bigl(\frac12,1\Bigr),\qquad 
M_{DA}\Bigl(0,\frac12\Bigr).
\]

For every vertex we draw the two segments that join it with the two
mid–points of the **opposite** sides.

---

### 1.   Equations of the eight lines  

\[
\begin{aligned}
& A\!M_{BC}:& y&=\tfrac12x \tag{1}\\[2pt]
& A\!M_{CD}:& y&=2x \tag{2}\\[2pt]
& B\!M_{CD}:& y&=-2x+2 \tag{3}\\[2pt]
& B\!M_{DA}:& y&=-\tfrac12x+\tfrac12 \tag{4}\\[2pt]
& C\!M_{DA}:& y&=\tfrac12x+\tfrac12 \tag{5}\\[2pt]
& C\!M_{AB}:& y&=2x-1 \tag{6}\\[2pt]
& D\!M_{AB}:& y&=-2x+1 \tag{7}\\[2pt]
& D\!M_{BC}:& y&=-\tfrac12x+1 \tag{8}
\end{aligned}
\]

Each line splits the square into two half‑planes.  
The octagon we need is the region that contains the centre of the square
\((\tfrac12,\tfrac12)\); in other words it is the intersection of the
following eight half‑planes:

\[
\begin{aligned}
&y\ge \tfrac12x ,\qquad &y\le 2x,\\
&y\le -2x+2 ,\qquad &y\ge -\tfrac12x+\tfrac12 ,\\
&y\le \tfrac12x+\tfrac12 ,\qquad &y\ge 2x-1 ,\\
&y\ge -2x+1 ,\qquad &y\le -\tfrac12x+1 .
\end{aligned}
\tag{9}
\]

---

### 2.   Vertices of the octagon  

The vertices are the intersection points of pairs of lines whose
corresponding inequalities are both tight in (9).  Solving the appropriate
pairs gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
&\bigl(\tfrac12,\tfrac14\bigr),\qquad\bigl(\tfrac34,\tfrac12\bigr),\qquad
\bigl(\tfrac12,\tfrac34\bigr),\qquad\bigl(\tfrac14,\tfrac12\bigr),\\[2pt]
&\bigl(\tfrac13,\tfrac13\bigr),\qquad\bigl(\tfrac23,\tfrac13\bigr),\qquad
\bigl(\tfrac23,\tfrac23\bigr),\qquad\bigl(\tfrac13,\tfrac23\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\tag{10}
\]

These eight points appear in the order  

\[
\Bigl(\tfrac12,\tfrac14\Bigr)\rightarrow
\Bigl(\tfrac23,\tfrac13\Bigr)\rightarrow
\Bigl(\tfrac34,\tfrac12\Bigr)\rightarrow
\Bigl(\tfrac23,\tfrac23\Bigr)\rightarrow
\Bigl(\tfrac12,\tfrac34\Bigr)\rightarrow
\Bigl(\tfrac13,\tfrac23\Bigr)\rightarrow
\Bigl(\tfrac14,\tfrac12\Bigr)\rightarrow
\Bigl(\tfrac13,\tfrac13\Bigr)
\]

which indeed forms a convex octagon (see the picture).

---

### 3.   Computing the area  

The octagon is the union of a small central square of side \(\tfrac13\)
and four congruent isosceles triangles.

* Central square: side \(=\tfrac13\);
  \[
  A_{\text{square}}=\Bigl(\tfrac13\Bigr)^2=\tfrac19 .
  \]

* One of the four triangles (the one at the bottom):
  its base is the segment from \((\tfrac13,\tfrac13)\) to
  \((\tfrac23,\tfrac13)\), so the base length is \(\tfrac13\).
  Its apex is \((\tfrac12,\tfrac14)\); the height is
  \(\tfrac13-\tfrac14=\tfrac1{12}\).
  Hence
  \[
  A_{\text{triangle}}=\frac12\cdot\frac13\cdot\frac1{12}
                     =\frac1{72}.
  \]
  There are four such triangles, so their total area is
  \(\displaystyle 4\cdot\frac1{72}=\frac1{18}\).

Adding the two parts,

\[
A_{\text{octagon}}
   =A_{\text{square}}+4A_{\text{triangle}}
   =\frac19+\frac1{18}
   =\frac2{18}+\frac1{18}
   =\boxed{\frac16}\text{ cm}^2 .
\]

---

### 4.   Alternative computation (shoelace)

If the eight vertices in the order shown above are substituted into the
shoelace formula, the same result \(\displaystyle\frac16\) is obtained.

Thus the octagon determined by joining each vertex of the unit square to
the mid‑points of the opposite sides has area \(\dfrac16\) square centimetre.<|eot_id|> <|end_of_text|>
